idiom_name: Akka Typed ActorRef[Order] (or Akka Streams Source[Order])
implementation_notes: In Akka Typed the channel is the ActorRef: spawning an actor with Behavior[Order] yields an ActorRef[Order] that accepts nothing else, so the actor's mailbox is a datatype channel and the handler never pattern-matches on a type tag - the protocol (a sealed trait hierarchy) is the message contract and the compiler checks it at every tell. Akka Streams expresses the same binding as typed sources and flows - Source[Order] with a per-type materialized pipeline and built-in back-pressure - which suits cases where the per-type channel is a stream to be transformed rather than one recipient's inbox. Choose the actor form when a single logical consumer owns the type's state; choose the stream form when the type flows through several stages.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Command
final case class PlaceOrder(order: Order) extends Command
final case class CancelOrder(id: OrderId) extends Command

val orders: ActorRef[Order] = context.spawn(OrderHandler(), "orders")
orders ! order                       // an Invoice would not compile
pitfalls: ActorRef[T] is contravariant: an ActorRef[Any] can be passed where ActorRef[Order] is expected, so widening the type silently reopens the mailbox to anything - keep the narrow protocol type in the public signature.
A typed actor still has an unbounded mailbox by default (and Streams still need a bounded buffer): the type binding says nothing about capacity, so back-pressure must be configured per type.
Serializing ActorRef[T] or protocol types across nodes depends on the serialization bindings; an unregistered message type fails at runtime, not at compile time.

variants.name: Akka Streams typed Source[T] per message type
variants.idiom_name: Akka Streams Source[Order] with per-type pipeline
variants.implementation_notes: The stream form keeps the type binding in the graph rather than in a mailbox: one Source[Order] (or per-type sub-stream) carried through typed Flows, with Reactive Streams back-pressure negotiated between stages. It fits channels whose payload is transformed on the way - enrich, split, aggregate - and where several stages must be composed at declaration time instead of one actor owning the state. The trade-off is that a stream is a closed graph: dynamic subscription, per-element acknowledgement and actor-style supervision must be re-added explicitly, which is exactly the ActorRef form's home ground.
variants.code_sketch:
val orders: Source[Order, NotUsed] = Source.fromPublisher(broker.ordersTopic)

orders
  .map(validate)
  .via(enrichCustomer)
  .runWith(Sink.foreachAsync(4)(handle))   // typed end to end, back-pressured
pitfalls: A materialized stream is a fixed graph: attaching a new consumer means rebuilding it, unlike an actor mailbox that new senders can reach at any time.
Backpressure only exists inside the graph - the boundary to a broker topic needs an explicitly configured buffer or overflow strategy, otherwise the per-type channel silently drops or grows.
